title: Single points of failure
summary: Find the one device and the one cable that would cut the office off, and give a switch a second way out.

sources.claim: Loops between Ethernet switches cause broadcast storms; spanning tree keeps redundant links in standby and uses them when the main path fails.
sources.cite: Juniper Networks, Spanning Tree Protocol Overview (Junos OS 25.4; the page shows no date)

steps.title: One box, many casualties
steps.body: A single point of failure is one device or one cable whose loss cuts others off. Every network has some. Finding them is how you decide which ones are worth a second path.

steps.title: The device
steps.prompt: Click the device that would cut off the most others if it failed.
steps.hint: Count what reaches fw-1 only through it.
steps.after: Every desk, the NAS, the Wi-Fi and both cameras reach fw-1 through switch-1. If it fails, the whole office is cut off.

steps.title: The cable
steps.prompt: Click the one cable that every desk's traffic crosses.
steps.after: The desk run, from switch-1 port 5 to switch-2 port 1. Cut it and desktop-1 and printer-1 lose the NAS and the internet.

steps.title: Walk the path
steps.prompt: Trace from desktop-1 to nas-1 and look at each hop.
steps.after: Each hop is one device or one cable, and none has a second way round.

steps.title: A second way out
steps.prompt: Checks has an idea about switch-3 in the meeting room: it has only one cable. Cable switch-3 port 2 to switch-2 port 4 and watch the idea clear.
steps.after: switch-3 can now lose one link and stay connected. On real switches a second link makes a loop, and loops cause broadcast storms, so switches run spanning tree, which keeps the extra link in standby until the main one fails.
